topics.title: Java Basics & OOP Fundamentals
topics.summary: Core Java syntax and the four pillars of object-oriented programming that everything else in Java builds on.
keyPoints: Encapsulation: bundling data and methods, controlling access with private/public/protected
Inheritance: 'extends' for reusing behavior; Java supports single inheritance of classes
Polymorphism: method overloading (compile-time) vs overriding (runtime)
Abstraction: abstract classes vs interfaces, and when to use each

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: An abstract class can have state (instance fields), constructors, and a mix of abstract and concrete methods, but a class can only extend one abstract class. An interface historically only declared method signatures and constants, but since Java 8 it can have default and static methods too; a class can implement multiple interfaces. Use an abstract class when subclasses share common state/implementation; use an interface to define a contract/capability across unrelated classes.
interviewQA.tip: Mention 'is-a' vs 'can-do' relationships and Java 8's default methods.

topics.title: Data Types, Variables & Type Casting
topics.summary: Java's strict static typing, primitive vs reference types, and rules for converting between them.
keyPoints: 8 primitive types (byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean) stored on the stack
Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, etc.) enable autoboxing/unboxing and use in collections
Widening (implicit) vs narrowing (explicit) casting
String immutability and the String pool

interviewQA.question: Why is String immutable in Java, and what problems could arise if it weren't?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: String is immutable so the JVM can safely cache identical literals in the String pool, saving memory. Immutability also makes String inherently thread-safe (no synchronization needed) and safe to use as a HashMap key since its hashCode never changes. If String were mutable, changing one reference could silently corrupt shared literals, break hash-based collections, and create security risks (e.g., a mutated URL or file path after validation).
interviewQA.tip: Bring up String pool and hashCode caching to show deeper understanding.

topics.title: Control Flow, Arrays & Loops
topics.summary: Decision-making and iteration constructs, plus how Java arrays behave as fixed-size objects.
keyPoints: if/else, switch (including Java 14+ switch expressions), for, while, do-while
Enhanced for-loop (for-each) for iterating collections and arrays
Arrays are fixed-length objects on the heap; default values differ by type
break/continue with labels for nested loop control

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between a traditional switch statement and a Java switch expression?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A traditional switch statement executes case blocks and falls through to the next case unless you add 'break'. A switch expression (Java 14+) uses arrow syntax (case X -> ...), returns a value directly, has no fall-through, and the compiler can enforce exhaustiveness for enums/sealed types. You use 'yield' inside a block-bodied case to return a value.
interviewQA.tip: Give a short code example contrasting fall-through risk vs arrow syntax.

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.summary: How Java models and recovers from errors using checked and unchecked exceptions.
keyPoints: Checked exceptions (must declare/catch) vs unchecked (RuntimeException) vs Errors
try-catch-finally and try-with-resources for AutoCloseable resources
Custom exceptions by extending Exception or RuntimeException
Exception chaining to preserve root cause

interviewQA.question: When would you create a checked exception vs an unchecked exception?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Use a checked exception when the caller can reasonably be expected to recover from the condition, such as a file not being found or a network timeout — forcing them to handle it is part of the API contract. Use an unchecked (runtime) exception for programming errors like invalid arguments or null references, where forcing every caller to catch it would add noise without real recovery options. Many modern APIs (like Spring) favor unchecked exceptions to avoid verbose try-catch chains.
interviewQA.tip: Reference how modern frameworks like Spring lean toward unchecked exceptions.

topics.title: Strings & String Manipulation
topics.summary: How Java stores and manipulates text, and why the difference between String, StringBuilder and StringBuffer matters for performance.
keyPoints: String is immutable; every concatenation with + creates a new object
StringBuilder is mutable and preferred for loops/heavy concatenation (not thread-safe)
StringBuffer is the synchronized, thread-safe equivalent of StringBuilder
Common methods: substring, split, trim, replace, equals vs ==

interviewQA.question: Why should you avoid using + to concatenate strings inside a loop?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Since String is immutable, each + creates a brand-new String object and discards the old one, so concatenating n times in a loop is O(n^2) and generates garbage for the collector. Using StringBuilder.append() mutates one internal buffer, making it O(n).
interviewQA.tip: Mention that the compiler already optimizes simple literal concatenation, but not loop-based concatenation.

topics.title: Java Memory Model Basics (Stack vs Heap)
topics.summary: Where Java objects and variables actually live at runtime, and why that matters for bugs like memory leaks and NullPointerExceptions.
keyPoints: Stack stores method call frames and local primitive/reference variables; heap stores actual objects
Each thread has its own stack, but the heap is shared across all threads
Objects with no remaining references become eligible for garbage collection
StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError indicate very different problems

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between a StackOverflowError and an OutOfMemoryError, and what usually causes each?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A StackOverflowError happens when the call stack exceeds its limit, almost always from unbounded or infinite recursion. An OutOfMemoryError happens when the heap can't allocate more objects, typically from a memory leak (objects that are still referenced but never needed again) or genuinely too much live data.
interviewQA.tip: Give a concrete example: a recursive function missing a base case for StackOverflowError, and a growing static List for OutOfMemoryError.

topics.title: Collections Framework
topics.summary: The core interfaces and implementations for storing and manipulating groups of objects, and how to choose between them.
keyPoints: List (ArrayList vs LinkedList), Set (HashSet, TreeSet, LinkedHashSet), Map (HashMap, TreeMap, LinkedHashMap)
Time complexity trade-offs: ArrayList O(1) get vs LinkedList O(1) insert at ends
Comparable vs Comparator for custom ordering
Fail-fast iterators and ConcurrentModificationException

interviewQA.question: How does HashMap work internally, and what changed with Java 8's implementation?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: HashMap stores entries in an array of buckets indexed by hashCode() % capacity, chaining colliding entries in a linked list. Since Java 8, if a single bucket's chain grows beyond a threshold (8 entries, with table size >= 64), it converts to a red-black tree, turning worst-case lookup from O(n) into O(log n). Resizing happens when size exceeds capacity * loadFactor (default 0.75), roughly doubling capacity and rehashing entries.
interviewQA.tip: Mention load factor 0.75 and the treeify threshold of 8 for a strong answer.

topics.title: Multithreading & Concurrency
topics.summary: Creating and coordinating threads safely, and the higher-level utilities that make it manageable.
keyPoints: Thread creation: extending Thread vs implementing Runnable/Callable
synchronized keyword, locks (ReentrantLock), and volatile for visibility
ExecutorService and thread pools instead of manual thread management
java.util.concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList)

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between synchronized and volatile, and when would you use each?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: 'volatile' guarantees visibility — a write by one thread is immediately visible to others — but does not provide atomicity or mutual exclusion, so it's suited for simple flags or single variables read/written independently. 'synchronized' provides both mutual exclusion (only one thread executes the block at a time) and visibility, making it appropriate for compound actions like check-then-act or updating multiple related fields together. Using volatile for a counter increment (i++) would still be unsafe because it's not atomic.
interviewQA.tip: Use the classic counter i++ example to show why volatile alone isn't enough.

topics.title: Java 8 Streams, Lambdas & Functional Interfaces
topics.summary: Functional-style processing of collections introduced in Java 8, and the lambda syntax that powers it.
keyPoints: Stream pipeline: source -> intermediate ops (map, filter, sorted) -> terminal op (collect, reduce, forEach)
Lazy evaluation: intermediate operations don't execute until a terminal operation is called
Functional interfaces: Function, Predicate, Supplier, Consumer, and method references
Collectors: toList, groupingBy, partitioningBy, joining

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between map() and flatMap() in Java Streams?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: map() transforms each element one-to-one, producing a stream of the same cardinality but a new type (e.g., String -> Integer). flatMap() is used when each element maps to its own stream (e.g., a List<List<String>>), and it flattens those inner streams into a single combined stream. A common example is flattening a list of orders each containing a list of items into one flat stream of items.
interviewQA.tip: Give a concrete example like List<List<Integer>> flattened with flatMap.

topics.title: JDBC, Spring Data & Database Connectivity
topics.summary: How Java applications talk to relational databases, from raw JDBC to Spring's abstractions.
keyPoints: JDBC core objects: DriverManager/DataSource, Connection, PreparedStatement, ResultSet
PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection and improves performance via precompilation
Connection pooling (HikariCP) to avoid the cost of opening connections per request
Spring Data JPA repositories abstract boilerplate CRUD and query methods

interviewQA.question: Why should you always prefer PreparedStatement over Statement?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: PreparedStatement takes parameterized input with placeholders (?), which are sent separately from the SQL text and never interpreted as executable SQL, closing off SQL injection attacks. It's also precompiled by the database, so repeated executions with different parameters are faster than a plain Statement that gets parsed and planned every time. Statement should really only be used for one-off DDL with no user input.
interviewQA.tip: Lead with the security angle (SQL injection) before performance.

topics.title: Generics & Wildcards
topics.summary: Type-safe, reusable code without casting, and how bounded wildcards make APIs both flexible and safe.
keyPoints: Generics catch type errors at compile time instead of ClassCastException at runtime
Bounded types: <T extends Number> restricts T to Number and its subclasses
Wildcards: ? extends T (read-only producer) vs ? super T (write-only consumer) — PECS rule
Type erasure means generic type info isn't available at runtime

interviewQA.question: Explain the PECS rule (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) with an example.
interviewQA.modelAnswer: PECS means: if a generic structure only produces (you read from it), use ? extends T; if it only consumes (you write to it), use ? super T. E.g. a copy method 'copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dest)' can read any subtype of T from src and safely write T into dest.
interviewQA.tip: Relate it back to Collections.copy()'s actual signature if you can recall it.

topics.title: Unit Testing with JUnit & Mockito
topics.summary: Writing isolated, repeatable tests for Java code, and mocking dependencies so tests don't hit real databases or APIs.
keyPoints: JUnit 5 annotations: @Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @ParameterizedTest
Assertions: assertEquals, assertThrows, assertTrue with descriptive messages
Mockito: @Mock creates a fake dependency, when()...thenReturn() stubs behavior, verify() checks interactions
Test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest end-to-end tests

interviewQA.question: Why would you mock a repository/DAO in a service-layer unit test instead of hitting a real database?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Mocking keeps the test focused on the service's own logic, makes it run in milliseconds instead of seconds, and removes flakiness caused by database state or network availability. Real database interaction belongs in a separate integration test layer.
interviewQA.tip: Mention verify(repository).save(any()) to show you also test interactions, not just return values.

topics.title: JVM Internals & Garbage Collection
topics.summary: How the JVM manages memory and how different garbage collectors trade off throughput, latency, and footprint.
keyPoints: Memory areas: heap (young/old gen), stack, metaspace, and where objects live
GC algorithms: Serial, Parallel, G1 (default since Java 9), ZGC/Shenandoah for low-latency
Minor GC (young gen, frequent) vs Major/Full GC (whole heap, expensive)
JVM tuning flags (-Xms, -Xmx, -XX:+UseG1GC) and analyzing GC logs

interviewQA.question: Walk through how an object typically moves through the JVM heap and gets garbage collected.
interviewQA.modelAnswer: New objects are allocated in Eden space within the young generation. When Eden fills up, a minor GC runs: live objects are copied to a Survivor space, and after surviving several minor GC cycles (tracked by an age counter), they're promoted to the Old generation. Old generation collections (major/full GC) are less frequent but more expensive since they scan a much larger region. Objects with no remaining references at any point become eligible for collection and their memory is reclaimed.
interviewQA.tip: Mention the generational hypothesis: most objects die young.

topics.title: Design Patterns in Java
topics.summary: Reusable solutions to common design problems, and how they map to real Java code you'll write daily.
keyPoints: Creational: Singleton, Factory, Builder (especially with Lombok's @Builder)
Structural: Adapter, Decorator, Proxy (used heavily by Spring AOP)
Behavioral: Strategy, Observer, Template Method
Dependency Injection as an application of Inversion of Control

interviewQA.question: How would you implement a thread-safe Singleton in modern Java, and what are the trade-offs of each approach?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: The simplest thread-safe approach is an eagerly initialized static field, which the JVM guarantees is initialized once, though it loses lazy loading. For lazy initialization with thread safety, double-checked locking with a volatile field avoids synchronization overhead on every access after first creation. The most robust option is an enum-based Singleton, which the JVM guarantees is instantiated exactly once and is inherently serialization-safe, though it's less flexible if you ever need inheritance.
interviewQA.tip: Mention enum singleton as the 'best practice' answer if pressed for one option.

topics.title: Spring Framework & Dependency Injection
topics.summary: How Spring's IoC container wires application components together and manages their lifecycle.
keyPoints: IoC container: beans, ApplicationContext, and component scanning
Dependency injection styles: constructor (preferred), setter, field injection
Bean scopes (singleton, prototype) and lifecycle callbacks (@PostConstruct)
Spring AOP for cross-cutting concerns like logging, transactions, security

interviewQA.question: Why is constructor injection generally preferred over field injection in Spring?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Constructor injection lets dependencies be declared as final fields, making the object immutable and impossible to construct in an incomplete state, which also makes circular dependencies fail fast at startup instead of silently at runtime. It makes unit testing straightforward since you can pass mocks directly into the constructor without needing a Spring context or reflection. Field injection (@Autowired on a field) hides dependencies, requires a DI framework or reflection to test, and allows objects to exist in a partially-initialized state.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that circular dependencies fail loudly at startup with constructor injection — a big plus.

topics.title: Microservices & Distributed Systems
topics.summary: Designing Java backends as independently deployable services and handling the distributed-systems problems that come with it.
keyPoints: Service decomposition, API gateways, and inter-service communication (REST, gRPC, messaging)
Resilience patterns: circuit breaker (Resilience4j), retries, timeouts, bulkheads
Distributed data challenges: eventual consistency, saga pattern for distributed transactions
Observability: centralized logging, distributed tracing, metrics

interviewQA.question: How would you handle a transaction that spans multiple microservices, given that distributed 2PC transactions don't scale well?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Instead of a two-phase commit, use the Saga pattern: break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each in its own service, with compensating actions defined to undo prior steps if a later step fails. Sagas can be coordinated via choreography (services react to each other's events) for simple flows, or orchestration (a central coordinator calls each step) for more complex flows needing clearer visibility. This trades strong consistency for eventual consistency, which is usually acceptable if the domain and UX account for it.
interviewQA.tip: Contrast choreography vs orchestration sagas explicitly — interviewers like this distinction.

topics.title: Reactive Programming (Project Reactor)
topics.summary: Non-blocking, backpressure-aware programming for high-throughput services, as used in Spring WebFlux.
keyPoints: Mono (0-1 result) and Flux (0-N results) are the two core reactive types
Operators like map, flatMap, filter build a pipeline that only executes on subscribe()
Backpressure lets a slow consumer signal a fast producer to slow down instead of overflowing
Reactive is best for I/O-bound, high-concurrency workloads, not CPU-bound work

interviewQA.question: What problem does backpressure solve, and how does Reactor handle it by default?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Backpressure prevents a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer with more data than it can process, which would otherwise cause unbounded buffering and OutOfMemoryErrors. Reactor's default strategy lets the subscriber request(n) items at a time, so the producer only emits what's been requested.
interviewQA.tip: Contrast reactive streams with traditional thread-per-request blocking I/O to show you understand the tradeoff.

topics.title: Java Performance Tuning & Profiling
topics.summary: Systematically finding and fixing performance bottlenecks in a running JVM application instead of guessing.
keyPoints: Use profilers (JFR, async-profiler, VisualVM) to find real hotspots before optimizing
JVM flags like -Xms/-Xmx set heap size; -XX:+UseG1GC selects the garbage collector
Common culprits: excessive object creation, N+1 queries, unindexed DB calls, synchronized contention
Measure before and after every change — intuition about 'slow code' is often wrong

interviewQA.question: A production service's p99 latency suddenly spiked. Walk through how you'd diagnose it.
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Check recent deploys/config changes first, then pull a thread dump to see if threads are blocked or stuck in GC, check GC logs for long pauses, and use a profiler or APM tool (e.g. JFR, Datadog) to find which method or downstream call is consuming the extra time under load.
interviewQA.tip: Mention correlating the spike with a specific traffic pattern or deploy timestamp.

topics: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a reviewer's feedback on your pull request
Describe handling a production bug that was introduced by your own code
How have you pushed back on an unrealistic sprint deadline from a PM

Tell me about mentoring a junior developer through a difficult bug
How do you handle being on-call for a service you didn't build
